title: Prepositions and Conjunctions: The Joining Words

blocks.text: "The committee discussed about the new fees." "My aunt is married with a doctor." "Please reply my letter." You hear all three every day in Nigeria, and all three would cost you marks. Prepositions cannot be worked out by logic — they are learned in fixed partnerships, and the exam tests exactly those partnerships.

blocks.markdown:
A **preposition** shows the relationship between a noun or pronoun and some other word in the sentence: the book *on* the desk, walked *towards* the gate, waited *until* dawn.

A **conjunction** joins words, phrases or clauses: rice *and* beans, tired *but* determined, stayed *because* it rained.

Both are small words that do heavy grammatical work, and both are heavily tested in Lexis and Structure.

blocks.title: Collocation
blocks.text: A fixed partnership between words that English speakers accept by convention rather than by rule — *accused of*, *congratulate on*, *prefer to*, *insist on*. Because no rule predicts them, collocations must be learned as whole units, exactly as you learn vocabulary.

blocks.title: Verbs that need no preposition at all
blocks.text: *Discuss*, *answer*, *enter*, *emphasise*, *request*, *lack* and *resemble* are transitive and take their object directly. Write "They discussed the report", not "discussed about the report"; "She entered the hall", not "entered into the hall"; "He emphasised the danger", not "emphasised on the danger".

blocks.markdown:
### Three kinds of conjunction

**Coordinating** — join units of equal rank. The seven are *for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so*. Each half could stand alone:
> She was exhausted, **but** she completed the race.

**Subordinating** — make one clause depend on another: *although, because, since, unless, until, while, if, whereas, as soon as, so that*. The subordinate clause cannot stand alone:
> **Although** he was ill, he wrote the paper.

**Correlative** — work in fixed pairs. Get the first member right and the second is decided for you:
> *either ... or*, *neither ... nor*, *both ... and*, *not only ... but also*, *no sooner ... than*, *hardly ... when*, *scarcely ... when*

blocks.title: Choosing the completion for a correlative structure
blocks.prompt: Complete the sentence: "Hardly had the closing bell rung ______ the pupils rushed out of the classroom."

steps.text: Identify the opening signal word. The sentence begins with *Hardly*, which is a correlative opener.
Recall the pair it belongs to. *Hardly* and *scarcely* are completed by *when*; only *no sooner* is completed by *than*.
Confirm the inverted structure that these openers demand: the auxiliary *had* comes before the subject *the closing bell*, which is correct here.
Insert *when* and read the sentence back: 'Hardly had the closing bell rung when the pupils rushed out of the classroom.'
Cross-check by rewriting with the other opener: 'No sooner had the closing bell rung than the pupils rushed out.' The two versions mean the same thing but use different partners.

blocks.answer: when — because *hardly* pairs with *when*, while *than* belongs to *no sooner*

blocks.title: One contrast marker per sentence
blocks.text: "Although he was ill, but he wrote the examination" uses two contrast markers to do one job. Choose one: "Although he was ill, he wrote the examination" or "He was ill, but he wrote the examination." The same rule applies to "Because ... therefore" and "Since ... so".

items: *Between* is used for two items and *among* for more than two.
*Beside* means next to; *besides* means in addition to.
*In* a town or country, but *at* a small precise point: in Ibadan, at Bodija junction.
*Since* marks a starting point in time; *for* marks a length of time: since 2019, for four years.
After a preposition, a verb takes the -ing form: *good at swimming*, *insisted on paying*.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: Build a personal list of collocations as you meet them, and always record the whole phrase — *deprived of*, not just *deprived*. In the exam, read the option aloud in your head; the correct partnership will usually sound familiar if you have met the phrase as a unit before.

points: Prepositions show relationships and are learned in fixed collocations, not derived from rules.
Some verbs, including discuss, answer, enter and emphasise, take no preposition at all.
Coordinating conjunctions join equal units; subordinating conjunctions make one clause dependent.
Correlative conjunctions come in fixed pairs, so the first member determines the second.
Never use two markers of the same relationship, as in *Although ... but*.
After any preposition, a following verb takes the -ing form.
